nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-01.title: Fill in the list
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-01.body:
In increasing order, the middle number is $75$. The mode $81$ must appear at least twice, and it is larger than the median, so the two largest numbers are $81, 81$. The range is $11$, so the smallest is $70$. The sum is $5\cdot76=380$, so the second smallest is $380-70-75-81-81=73$.

**Answer: 73**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-02.title: Glue the O's
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-02.body:
Treat $OOO$ as one block. We arrange 5 items $C, C, R, S, [OOO]$ with $C$ repeated: $\frac{5!}{2!}=60$.

**Answer: 60**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-03.title: Perfect squares
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-03.body:
Divisors pair up as $d$ and $\frac nd$; the count is odd exactly when $n$ is a perfect square. Since $44^2=1936<2007<2025=45^2$, there are $44$ such numbers.

**Answer: 44**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-04.title: Combine the conditions
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-04.body:
Let the roots be $r$ and $-r$ (additive inverses). Being multiplicative inverses, $r\cdot(-r)=1$, so $r^2=-1$ and $r=\pm i$. The roots are $i$ and $-i$ (with $a=0$, $b=1$).

**Answer: $\pm i$**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-05.title: Substitute
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-05.body:
$x^2=y^2$, so $5x^2=1$ and $x=\pm\frac1{\sqrt5}$, $y=\pm\frac1{\sqrt5}$ with independent signs: $4$ points.

**Answer: 4**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-05.title: Picture
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-05.body:
The first graph is the pair of lines $y=\pm x$ through the origin; the second is an ellipse centered at the origin. Each line passes through the center and meets the ellipse twice, giving $4$ points.

**Answer: 4**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-06.title: Centroid ratios
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-06.body:
$F$ is the centroid, so $AF=2FD$ and $BF=2FE$. Since $AF=BF=10$, $FD=FE=5$. In triangle $AFE$, $\angle AFE=180^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ$, so
$$AE^2=10^2+5^2-2\cdot10\cdot5\cos120^\circ=175,\quad AE=5\sqrt7,$$
and $AC=2AE=10\sqrt7$. By symmetry $BC=10\sqrt7$. The perimeter is $10+20\sqrt7$.

**Answer: $10+20\sqrt7$**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-06.title: Coordinates
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-06.body:
Let $A=(-5,0)$, $B=(5,0)$, $F=(0,5\sqrt3)$. The centroid is the average of the vertices, so $C=3F-A-B=(0,15\sqrt3)$. Then $AC=\sqrt{25+675}=\sqrt{700}=10\sqrt7=BC$, and the perimeter is $10+20\sqrt7$.

**Answer: $10+20\sqrt7$**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-07.title: Perpendicular bisector
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-07.body:
The perpendicular bisector of the segment from $(0,0)$ to $(2,6)$ passes through $(1,3)$ with slope $-\frac13$: $y-3=-\frac13(x-1)$. Setting $y=0$: $x=10$.

**Answer: 10**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-09.title: Area two ways
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-09.body:
The diagonals bisect each other at right angles, so the side is $\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$. The area is $\frac12\cdot6\cdot8=24$, and also equals side $\times$ height, so the height is $\frac{24}5$. The inscribed circle's diameter is the height, so $r=\frac{12}5$.

**Answer: $\frac{12}{5}$**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-09.title: Altitude in a right triangle
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-09.body:
The radius is the distance from the center to a side, i.e. the altitude to the hypotenuse of the 3-4-5 right triangle formed by half-diagonals: $\frac{3\cdot4}{5}=\frac{12}5$.

**Answer: $\frac{12}{5}$**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-10.title: Same base
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-10.body:
$\log_4(x+2)=\frac12\log_2(x+2)$, so $\log_2(x+2)=2\log_2(2x-1)$, i.e. $x+2=(2x-1)^2$ with $2x-1>0$. Then $4x^2-5x-1=0$ and $x=\frac{5\pm\sqrt{41}}8$. Only $\frac{5+\sqrt{41}}8\approx1.43$ satisfies $x>\frac12$.

**Answer: $\frac{5+\sqrt{41}}{8}$**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-11.title: Ratio of areas at C
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-11.body:
Triangles $CDE$ and $CAB$ share angle $C$, so
$$\frac{[CDE]}{[CAB]}=\frac{CD}{CA}\cdot\frac{CE}{CB}=\frac25\cdot\frac16=\frac1{15}.$$
Thus $[CDE]=\frac{75}{15}=5$.

**Answer: 5**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-12.title: Tail of the series
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-12.body:
The terms after the third sum to $\frac12-\frac16=\frac13$, and this tail is $r^3$ times the whole series: $r^3\cdot\frac12=\frac13$, so $r^3=\frac23$ and $r=\frac{\sqrt[3]{18}}3$.

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt[3]{18}}{3}$**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-13.title: Subtract the inside
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-13.body:
The unpainted cubes form the inner $8\times8\times8$ cube: $512$. So $1000-512=488$ have paint.

**Answer: 488**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-14.title: Set up equations
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-14.body:
With first term $a$ and difference $d$: $5a+10d=(a+5d)+(a+6d)$, so $3a=d$. Then $a+3d=10a=70$, $a=7$, $d=21$, and the second term is $28$.

**Answer: 28**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-16.title: Distance from the center
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-16.body:
Put the semicircle's center $O$ at the origin with its diameter on the $x$-axis. Each small circle touches the diameter and the other circle, so their centers are $(\pm5,5)$. Each small circle is internally tangent to the arc, so $r$ equals the distance from $O$ to a small center plus $5$: $r=5\sqrt2+5$.

**Answer: $5\sqrt2+5$**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-18.title: Choose four digits
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-18.body:
The digits are distinct, and $A\ge1$ is the smallest, so all four come from $\{1,\dots,9\}$. Any choice of 4 digits gives exactly one snaking number (smallest $=A$, then $C$, $B$, largest $=D$). So there are $\binom94=126$.

**Answer: 126**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-20.title: Zero discriminant
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-20.body:
Exactly one real solution means a double root: $k^2-8k=0$, so $k=0$ (root $0$) or $k=8$ (root $-4$).

**Answer: $k=0,\ 8$**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-21.title: Square both sides
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-21.body:
$j=(8+\sqrt{15})+(8-\sqrt{15})-2\sqrt{64-15}=16-14=2$ (the left side is positive, so squaring is safe).

**Answer: 2**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-24.title: Area formulas
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-24.body:
$s=9$, and by Heron the area is $K=\sqrt{9\cdot1\cdot1\cdot7}=3\sqrt7$. Then $r=\frac Ks=\frac{\sqrt7}{3}$ and $R=\frac{abc}{4K}=\frac{128}{12\sqrt7}=\frac{32}{3\sqrt7}$. So $\frac Rr=\frac{32}{3\sqrt7}\cdot\frac3{\sqrt7}=\frac{32}7$.

**Answer: $\frac{32}{7}$**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-25.title: Quadratic
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-25.body:
$\frac{x+2}{2}=\frac2x$, so $x^2+2x-4=0$ and $x=-1\pm\sqrt5$. The positive root is $-1+\sqrt5$.

**Answer: $-1+\sqrt5$**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-26.title: Pairs of lines
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-26.body:
Two lines meet in at most one point. With no two parallel and no three concurrent, every pair gives a different point: $\binom92=36$.

**Answer: 36**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-28.title: Differences
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-28.body:
Equal remainders mean $x$ divides the differences $344-228=116$ and $518-228=290$. The largest such $x$ is $\gcd(116,290)=58$. Check: the remainders are all $54$.

**Answer: 58**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-29.title: Factor and check the domain
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-29.body:
$\sqrt{x-6}\,(1-x)=0$, so $\sqrt{x-6}=0$ or $x=1$. For real square roots we need $x\ge6$, which rules out $x=1$ (it would give $\sqrt{-5}$). So $x=6$, where both sides are $0$.

**Answer: $x=6$**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-30.title: Discriminant in x
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-30.body:
As a quadratic in $x$: $2x^2-\sqrt3y\,x+(y^2-1)=0$. A real solution exists iff $3y^2-8(y^2-1)\ge0$, i.e. $y^2\le\frac85$. The maximum is $y=\sqrt{\frac85}=\frac{2\sqrt{10}}5$.

**Answer: $\frac{2\sqrt{10}}{5}$**

nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-30.title: Cauchy–Schwarz
nyciml-2006-07-spring-seniorb-30.body:
Solving for $y$: $2y=\sqrt3x+\sqrt{4-5x^2}$ (larger root). By Cauchy–Schwarz, $\sqrt3\,x+1\cdot\sqrt{4-5x^2}=\sqrt{\tfrac35}\cdot\sqrt5x+1\cdot\sqrt{4-5x^2}\le\sqrt{\left(\tfrac35+1\right)\left(5x^2+4-5x^2\right)}=\sqrt{\tfrac{32}5}$. So $y\le\frac12\sqrt{\frac{32}5}=\frac{2\sqrt{10}}5$, with equality when $x=\frac{\sqrt{30}}{10}$.

**Answer: $\frac{2\sqrt{10}}{5}$**
